How to Plan Your Next Move at Mid-Career Rakesh Verma 5 min read · Sep 25, 2026 -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size At some point in your career, you may find yourself thinking: “Is this really what I want to continue doing?” You may have a good job, years of experience and a stable career. Yet something may not feel right anymore. Perhaps you are no longer learning. Maybe the work doesn’t excite you as it once did. Or your priorities have changed, and you are wondering what you want from the next phase of your career. A career change at 35, 40 or 50 can feel very different from making a career decision early in your working life. You have experience, relationships, credibility and a professional identity to consider. So the question isn’t always “How do I start again?” It may be: “How can I use what I have already built to create a better next chapter?” You May Not Need to Start From Scratch A career change doesn’t always mean leaving your industry or starting in a completely new field. Sometimes, the change you need is smaller. A sales professional may move into strategic accounts or business development. A finance professional may move towards business strategy, analytics or transformation. A functional leader may want broader business responsibility rather than a completely different career. Your experience can become the bridge to your next opportunity. Before deciding to start over, ask yourself: What can I carry forward, and what really needs to change? Press enter or click to view image in full size First Understand What You Want to Change Sometimes we say, “I need a career change,” when the real issue is something else. Maybe it is your organisation. Maybe it is your manager. Maybe you have stopped growing. Maybe you want more meaningful work. Maybe you want greater responsibility or simply a different kind of challenge. These are different problems and may require different solutions. Taking time to understand what is actually bothering you can prevent you from making a major decision based only on temporary frustration. Look Beyond Your Job Title At mid-career, your job title is only one part of your professional value. Think about what you have learned to do over the years. You may have developed strengths in: Leading teams Managing stakeholders Building relationships Solving problems Negotiating and influencing Making decisions Managing customers Developing people Handling difficult situations These capabilities can travel with you. Instead of asking only: “What job should I apply for?” also ask: “What am I good at, and where else could these strengths create value?” This can open up possibilities you may not have considered. Press enter or click to view image in full size Keep Learning Without Throwing Away Your Experience The world of work is changing, and technology — including AI — is changing many roles. That doesn’t mean you need to become a technology expert. It does mean you may need to understand how technology is affecting your profession and what new skills could make your experience more relevant. The question is not simply: “Do I need to learn AI?” It is: “What do I need to learn to make my existing experience more valuable?” That is a much more practical way to approach learning during a career transition. Your Next Move May Be Within Your Current Organisation Career change is often imagined as resignation followed by a completely new job. But sometimes the change you need is closer than you think. An internal move, a new project, a cross-functional role or a new business responsibility can give you a different challenge without throwing away the professional capital you have built. It can also help you test whether you genuinely want a different career — or simply need a different environment. Don’t Make a Career Decision Only to Escape When work becomes frustrating, it is natural to think: “I just want to get out.” But moving away from something is not the same as moving towards something. Before making a major career decision, ask yourself: What am I trying to move away from? What do I want more of in my working life? What strengths do I want to use more often? What skills do I need to develop? What would make the next phase of my career meaningful? You don’t need to have all the answers immediately. But you do need enough clarity to take the next step consciously. Your Experience Should Inform Your Next Chapter A mid-career change is not about proving that you can start again. It is about understanding what you have built — and deciding how you want to use it next. Your experience still has value. Your skills still have value. But your definition of success may have changed. So before asking: “What should I do next?” ask yourself: “What do I want my next chapter to look like?” A thoughtful career transition doesn’t always begin with a new job. It often begins with clarity. And when you have greater clarity about what you want, what you bring and what needs to change, your next move becomes easier to make.
